title: Daily volume from a trades table
objectives: Summarise fills by day and ticker with `GROUP BY date, ticker`
Compute traded value and VWAP with `SUM(qty * price)`
Sort groups by an aggregate, and preview a daily return with `LAG`

byKey.whole-day: You took every fill on 12 March, BARC's included. The group is one ticker on one day.

widget.solution:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE trades(id INTEGER, date TEXT, ticker TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    (1, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 200, 118.90),
    (2, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 5000, 2.17),
    (3, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 500, 119.20),
    (4, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 8000, 2.19),
    (5, "2024-03-13", "AZN", 300, 117.80),
    (6, "2024-03-13", "AZN", 100, 117.50),
    (7, "2024-03-13", "BARC", 6000, 2.16),
    (8, "2024-03-13", "AZN", 400, 117.70),
])


def query():
    return """
SELECT date, ticker, SUM(qty) AS volume
FROM trades
GROUP BY date, ticker
ORDER BY date, ticker
"""

screens.title: The busiest day
screens.prose:
```sql
SELECT date, ticker, SUM(qty) AS volume
FROM trades
GROUP BY date, ticker
ORDER BY volume DESC
LIMIT 1;
```
screens.question: Which row comes back?

options.why: You sorted single fills. `ORDER BY` runs after grouping, so it sorts the daily totals.
AZN on 13 March is the biggest day in pounds, not in shares. This query sorts by `volume`, a share count.

hints.text: Work out the four daily volumes first.
They are 700, 13,000, 800 and 6,000 shares.
The largest is BARC on 12 March.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort the four daily totals, largest first.

explain.text: `ORDER BY volume DESC` sorts the finished groups by their own aggregate, and `LIMIT 1` keeps the top one. BARC wins on shares because its price is about £2.

screens.title: Traded value
screens.prose: Risk now wants each day and ticker's **traded value** in pounds: what all its fills cost.
screens.question: Which expression gives it?

options.why: You multiplied total shares by the average price. `AVG` weights a 200-share fill like a 500-share one, so AZN on 12 March comes out at £83,335, not £83,380.

canvas.caption: AVG(price) gives each fill the same weight

options.why: Adding the prices of two fills gives £238.10, which is not a price at all. It roughly doubles the value.

hints.text: What did each fill cost on its own?
One fill costs its `qty` times its `price`.
Multiply inside each row, then add the products.

feedback.correct: Each fill is priced at its own price, then the costs are added.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each fill first, then add.

byKey.avg: You multiplied total shares by the average price. `AVG` weights a 200-share fill like a 500-share one, so AZN on 12 March comes out at £83,335, not £83,380.

explain.text: AZN on 12 March: 200 × £118.90 + 500 × £119.20 = £83,380. The shortcut with `AVG(price)` gives £83,335, because it ignores that the bigger fill had the higher price.

screens.title: VWAP
screens.prose:
The **volume-weighted average price**, VWAP, is traded value over volume. Traders judge their fills against it.

```sql
SUM(qty * price) / SUM(qty)
```
screens.question: What is AZN's VWAP on 12 March? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: You found the traded value on the last screen.
It is £83,380 over 700 shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the traded value by the volume.

byKey.avg: You took the plain average of the two prices. VWAP weights the 500-share fill more than the 200-share one.
byKey.value: That is the traded value. Divide it by the 700 shares.

explain.text: VWAP is £83,380 / 700 = £119.11, above the plain average of £119.05. The bigger fill was at the higher price, so it pulls the average up.

screens.title: Yesterday's close
screens.prose:
A daily return needs yesterday's close beside today's. A **window function** fetches it without folding any rows.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, close,
  LAG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY date)
FROM prices;
```

state.caption: prices, sorted by ticker then date

screens.question: Tap the close that `LAG(close)` returns on BARC's 13 March row.

hints.text: `LAG` looks back one row.
`PARTITION BY ticker` keeps BARC's rows apart from AZN's.
One row back from BARC on 13 March is BARC on 12 March.

feedback.correct: BARC closed at £2.18 the day before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step back one day inside BARC's own rows.

byKey.r5c2: That is the row's own close. `LAG` reaches one row back.
byKey.r3c2: That is two days back. `LAG(close)` reaches one row back.
byKey.r2c2: That is an AZN close. `PARTITION BY ticker` keeps each ticker's rows apart.

explain.text: `LAG(close)` reaches one row back within the ticker, in date order, so BARC on 13 March sees £2.18. Its return is 2.15 / 2.18 − 1 ≈ −1.38%. Each ticker's first day has no row behind it, so `LAG` gives `NULL` there.

screens.title: Two shapes of summary
screens.prose:
A `GROUP BY` folds each group into one row. A window function keeps every row and adds a value from its neighbours.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker,
  ROUND(close / LAG(close) OVER
    (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY date) - 1, 4)
FROM prices;
```
screens.question: What does this give on AZN's first day, 11 March?

options.why: You read "no earlier close" as "no change". There is no earlier close at all, so the division has nothing to use.
Arithmetic with `NULL` gives `NULL` in SQL. Nothing fails, which is why the first row needs care later.

feedback.correct: No previous close, so no return.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what `LAG` returns on the first row of a ticker.

explain.text: `LAG` gives `NULL` on each ticker's first row, and `close / NULL` is `NULL`. A table of daily returns always starts one row short per ticker.

screens.title: Write the report
screens.prose: A daily report needs volumes from 12 March on, days of at least 1,000 shares only, biggest first. SQL fixes the order in which you write the clauses.
screens.question: Put the lines of the query in the order you must write them.

hints.text: `SELECT` is written first, even though the database works on it late.
The row filter comes before the grouping; the group filter after.
`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `ORDER BY`.

feedback.correct: Written order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with `SELECT`, then follow the order the database works in.

explain.text: You write `SELECT` first, then the clauses in the order the database runs them. `ORDER BY` can use the name `volume` because it runs after `SELECT` defines it.

screens.prose: Commission is charged on traded value, not on shares. The desk head wants each ticker's traded value over both days, largest first.
screens.question: Return each ticker with its traded value rounded to 2 places, sorted by traded value, largest first.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE trades(id INTEGER, date TEXT, ticker TEXT, qty INTEGER, price REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    (1, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 200, 118.90),
    (2, "2024-03-12", "BARC", 5000, 2.17),
    (3, "2024-03-12", "AZN", 500, 119.20),

The value of a fill is `qty * price`; sum those per ticker.
`SELECT ticker, ROUND(SUM(qty * price), 2) AS value FROM trades GROUP BY ticker ORDER BY value DESC`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the examples and compare your rows with the expected ones.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[('AZN', 177550.0), ('BARC', 41330.0)]`. Check `SUM(qty * price)` and the sort direction.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds a £220,000 BARC fill, so BARC must now come first. Sort by the value, not by name.

explain.text: BARC traded far more shares, but AZN traded over four times the money. Sorting by `SUM(qty * price)` ranks tickers by what commission is charged on.

ideas: Grouping by `date, ticker` gives one row per ticker per day; `SUM(qty)` is that day's volume.
Traded value is `SUM(qty * price)`: price each fill, then add. VWAP divides it by `SUM(qty)`.
`ORDER BY` runs last, so it can sort groups by an aggregate; `LAG` adds the previous row's value without folding rows.

formula.name: VWAP
formula.note: In SQL: `SUM(qty * price) / SUM(qty)` per group.

summary.trap: `SUM(qty) * AVG(price)` is not the traded value: it weights a small fill as much as a large one.

quiz.prose:
A query lists daily traded value per ticker and sorts by it.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, SUM(qty * price) AS value
FROM trades
GROUP BY date, ticker
ORDER BY value DESC;
```
quiz.question: When does the database sort?

options.text: After grouping, on the finished totals

options.why: You expected `ORDER BY` to sort the raw rows. It runs last, on the rows the groups produce.

options.text: Never: `value` is not a column of `trades`
options.why: `AS value` names a result column, and `ORDER BY` runs after `SELECT`, so the name is known.

feedback.correct: `ORDER BY` runs last, on the grouped rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the order in which the clauses run.

explain.text: `ORDER BY` is the last step, after `SELECT` has made one row per group. So it sorts the totals, and it can use the name `value`.

quiz.prose:
BARC closed at £2.18 on 12 March and £2.15 on 13 March.

```sql
ROUND(close / LAG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY date) - 1, 4)
```
quiz.question: What does this give on BARC's 13 March row?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide today's close by yesterday's, then subtract 1.

byKey.flipped: You divided yesterday by today. The return is today over yesterday, minus 1.
byKey.pct: That is the percentage. The query returns the decimal, −0.0138.

explain.text: `LAG(close)` is £2.18, so the return is 2.15 / 2.18 − 1 = −0.01376, which rounds to −0.0138 at four places.
